options: A chunk of a DataFrame's data held in memory on one Executor
A directory on disk, like year=2024/month=01/
A synonym for a Worker Node
A type of file format
questions.explain: This is completely unrelated to Lesson 9's storage partitioning, despite sharing the same word.

questions.q: How is the number of partitions for a newly-read DataFrame typically determined?
options: Spark automatically splits the data based roughly on file size and number of files
It is always fixed at exactly 1, regardless of data size
The user must manually count every row before reading
Partitions only exist after calling a specific action, never on read
questions.explain: This automatic splitting is what gives Spark something to parallelize across Executors from the start.

questions.q: What happens if a DataFrame has far fewer partitions than available Executor cores?
options: Many cores sit idle, since each Task processes exactly one partition and there aren't enough partitions to use every core
Spark automatically creates more Executors to compensate
The job fails immediately with an error
Nothing changes — partition count has no effect on parallelism
questions.explain: This is the 'too few partitions' problem — a cluster bigger than the job can actually use.

questions.q: What happens if a DataFrame has far too many, tiny partitions?
options: Each partition's own small scheduling/coordination overhead can add up, spending more time managing partitions than doing real work
The job automatically merges them with no downside
Too many partitions always makes a job faster with no tradeoff
Spark refuses to process a DataFrame with more than 100 partitions
questions.explain: This is the opposite problem from too few — overhead outweighing the benefit of finer-grained parallelism.

questions.q: What is the relationship between a Task and a Spark partition?
options: A Task is the unit of work an Executor runs, and it processes exactly one partition
A Task and a partition are exactly the same thing with different names
One partition is always processed by multiple Tasks simultaneously
Tasks and partitions have no relationship to each other
questions.explain: This one-to-one relationship between Task and partition is genuinely how Spark achieves parallelism.
